953.title: Vasudeva in the jail cell
953.hook: a prisoner looks at the bars of his cell and sees Krishna
953.carry: vasudeva is everything, even the bars
953.howItsDone: Some followers of Sri Aurobindo read his speeches, letters and books as part of daily practice, and his ashram in Puducherry and centers elsewhere hold collective meditation and study of his writings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's shade: happiness isn't in things, and the wise one joy is the self's own, not the thing's.

A jail cell in Calcutta, and a prisoner waiting for his trial. He'd been a writer and a political leader, arguing hard for India's freedom from British rule, and now he's accused in a bombing case. He's allowed very little. One of the few things he has is a copy of the Bhagavad Gita. Later, after he walked out free, he gave a speech about what happened to him in that cell. His name was Aurobindo Ghose. People came to know him as Sri Aurobindo.
screen: `A CELL IN CALCUTTA.` → `A TRIAL, AND A GITA.` → `A SPEECH, AFTER RELEASE.`

segments.voice: In the speech, Aurobindo says he had asked God for guidance before his arrest, and in jail he felt the answer came. He was given the Gita, and he was asked, as he tells it, to live what it teaches, not just read it. Then something changed in how he saw. He looked at the walls that held him, and they were no longer walls. It was Vasudeva, a name for Krishna, standing around him. The tree in the yard: Vasudeva. The bars of the cell, the grating on the door: Vasudeva again. He looked at the other prisoners, thieves and men accused of murder, and found Vasudeva in them too. Even in court, looking at the prosecutor arguing to convict him, he saw the same presence. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, said plainly: God is in everything and everyone. The Gita puts it in three words, vasudevah sarvam, Vasudeva is everything, and Krishna says the one who sees him in everything, and everything in him, is never lost to him. Aurobindo is describing what it was like when that line stopped being an idea. And notice where it happened. Not in a temple. In a jail, among accused men, facing the man trying to convict him. It's also how many Hindus read the everyday namaste, palms together: a bow to the divine in the other person, whoever they are.
screen: `IN JAIL, HE WAS GIVEN THE GITA.` · `THE WALLS, THE TREE, THE BARS: VASUDEVA.` · `EVEN THE PRISONERS. EVEN THE PROSECUTOR.` · `VASUDEVA IS EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `GOD IN EVERYONE. NAMASTE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something ordinary in front of you, a wall, a window frame, a cup, and look at it slowly before moving on to the next thing, and the next. If you pray, hold each one as Aurobindo held the walls of his cell, as a place where God is; if you don't, give each thing the attention you'd give something precious. Last, bring to mind one person you find hard, and hold them there too, and in your mind fold your hands to them: namaste.
Aurobindo. The writer and freedom fighter who, by his own account, saw Krishna in the walls, the bars and the prisoners of his jail.
Your line: Vasudeva is everything, even the bars. Tomorrow, why he left politics, and the four words he built a whole yoga on. That's day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: All life is yoga
954.hook: an inner command, a boat to Pondicherry, and yoga in the kitchen
954.carry: all life is yoga, so offer what you do
954.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes food is offered at the shrine before it is eaten as prasad, and those who follow Sri Aurobindo's integral yoga try to offer their daily work, relationships and study in the same spirit; at the Pondicherry ashram, everyday work is treated as part of the practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo in his cell: Vasudeva is everything, even the bars and the man prosecuting him.

Calcutta, early in 1910. Aurobindo has been out of jail less than a year, and word comes that the police mean to arrest him again. He says he heard an inner command, adesh, he called it: go to Chandernagore, a French town up the river. Within minutes, the story goes, he was on a boat. A few weeks later he sailed south to Pondicherry, another French town, and stayed there the rest of his life. The fiery political leader was gone. So did he go off to sit in a cave?
screen: `CALCUTTA, 1910: AN INNER COMMAND.` → `A BOAT, THEN PONDICHERRY.` → `OFF TO A CAVE?`

segments.voice: No. In Pondicherry he wrote the book that sets out his way, The Synthesis of Yoga, and near its start stand four words: all life is yoga. Not some of life. All of it: the cooking, the job, the argument, the walk home. Behind it stands one of the Gita's great teachings. Krishna tells Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. That's karma yoga, the yoga of work: action given to God. The Gita also speaks of bhakti, the yoga of love, and jnana, the yoga of knowledge. Aurobindo doesn't make anyone choose. He gathers all three into one practice and calls it integral yoga. Then he goes a step further. Some paths, he says, aim to rise out of the world. His aim is for the divine to come down into it and change it: body, mind, ordinary life. Yesterday's cell sits underneath this. If Vasudeva can stand in prison walls, no chore is too low to be part of the yoga. You can see the teaching in an ordinary Hindu kitchen. In many homes, food is cooked for God and offered at the shrine first, as bhog or naivedya, and only then eaten as prasad, blessed food. Other Hindu teachers read life's final goal differently. Aurobindo's word to that long conversation was simple: don't leave. Bring it all in.

955.title: Aurobindo's Savitri
955.hook: an old story you already know, retold as a legend and a symbol
955.carry: savitri's steady love wins life back from death
955.howItsDone: On Vat Savitri, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women fast, wind thread around a banyan tree and pray for their husbands' long life; some followers of Sri Aurobindo also read his Savitri aloud, a few lines at a time, as a daily spiritual reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's four words: all life is yoga, so offer what you do, so offer what you do, even the cooking.
screen: `AUROBINDO.` · `ALL LIFE IS YOGA, SO OFFER WHAT YOU DO.`

segments.voice: A princess named Savitri chooses Satyavan for her husband, though she's told he will die within the year. On the day it comes, they're in the forest together, he lays his head in her lap, and Death himself arrives to carry him off. And Savitri gets up and follows Death. Earlier this year you heard that story as the Mahabharata tells it. Aurobindo heard something more in it, and turned it into a long poem of his own.
screen: `SAVITRI CHOOSES SATYAVAN.` → `DEATH COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `SHE GETS UP AND FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: He called the poem Savitri, and gave it a subtitle: a legend and a symbol. In a note at its front, he explains. The Mahabharata tells the tale as married love conquering death, and he doesn't deny that. But he reads each person in it as standing for something larger too. Satyavan is the soul that carries the divine truth inside it, but has come down into the grip of death and ignorance. Savitri is the divine Word, daughter of the Sun, come down to be born and to save. Her father, the king who prayed so long for a child, stands for tapasya, the long human effort that reaches from the mortal toward the immortal. Put that beside yesterday's four words. If all life is yoga, and the divine comes down to change life rather than flee it, then Savitri is that hope told as a story. She doesn't climb out of the world to escape death. She walks after Death, speaks to him of dharma, and won't let go until life is given back. His reading doesn't replace the old tale; it holds a second lamp up to it. And the old tale isn't only read, it's kept. Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep Vat Savitri: they fast, wind thread around a banyan tree, the tree where, as the tradition tells it, Satyavan lay with his head in her lap, and pray for their husbands' long life. A wife's steadiness, kept as a vow.
screen: `A LEGEND AND A SYMBOL.` · `SATYAVAN: THE SOUL, HELD BY DEATH.` · `SAVITRI: THE DIVINE WORD, COME TO SAVE.` · `VAT SAVITRI: A FAST, A BANYAN, A THREAD.` · then, large: `SHE WALKS AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love whose life or health you worry about, and see them clearly, the way Savitri saw Satyavan with his head in her lap. Then, with each breath, hold them steadily, without letting go, the way the women at the banyan wind the thread around it again and again. If you pray, pray for their long life in your own words; if you don't, simply wish them well, breath by breath.

956.title: Gandhi meets the Gita
956.hook: a young law student is embarrassed to admit he hasn't read the Gita
956.carry: dwelling on a want slides into anger
956.howItsDone: In Gandhian ashrams the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the one of steady wisdom, are recited as part of daily prayer, and some Hindus learn Gita verses by heart, a few at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurobindo's Savitri, a legend and a symbol: Savitri's steady love wins life back from Death, and women still keep her fast at the banyan.

London, and a young Indian law student far from home. Two brothers he's met, Theosophists interested in Indian thought, are reading the Bhagavad Gita in an English translation, Edwin Arnold's verse version, and they invite him to read the original with them. And the young man has to admit something awkward. He has never read it. Not in Sanskrit, not in his own Gujarati. He tells this story about himself later, in his autobiography, and he says he felt ashamed. The young man was Mohandas Gandhi.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `TWO BROTHERS AND A GITA.` → `HE HAD NEVER READ IT.`

segments.voice: So Gandhi's Gita begins in an unlikely place: friends from another country, an English verse translation, and a Sanskrit text he could only half follow. He reads it with them, and some verses near the end of the second chapter strike him hard. They hold one of the Gita's best-known teachings: how a want takes over a mind, step by step. A person dwells on the things the senses want. From dwelling comes attachment. From attachment, desire. From desire, anger. From anger, confusion. Memory slips, judgment fails, and the person is lost. Gandhi doesn't say he understood all of it then. But the book stayed with him, and he came to prize it above other books for knowing truth. Later, in South Africa, he did something very ordinary with it. He wrote verses on slips of paper, stuck them on the wall where he washed in the morning, and learned them by heart while getting ready for the day. Not in a temple. Next to the washbasin. The same chapter describes the one the Gita calls sthitaprajna, whose wisdom stands steady, who sees the slide starting and isn't carried off by every want and every fear. Those verses became part of the daily prayers in the community he founded. Gandhi didn't arrive with the Gita already in hand. He came to it a little late, a little embarrassed, and then he kept it close.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want tugging at you today, a snack, a scroll, a reply you'd like to send, and watch the slide the Gita describes, slowly: the dwelling, the pull of it, the wanting, without scolding yourself. Then let the attention rest on the breath, steady, the way the steady one in the Gita stays still while the wants come and go. If you pray, you can hold that steadiness in prayer.

957.title: The battlefield inside
957.hook: a book that opens on a battlefield, read by a man of nonviolence
957.howItsDone: Readers of Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga often read the Gita's battle as a picture of the struggle within, and some Hindus keep a short daily reading of the Gita alongside their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhi met the Gita as a law student in London, and its slide stayed with him: dwelling on a want slides into anger.

Two armies face each other on an open field. Conch shells sound across the lines. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive out into the gap between them. He looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His bow slips from his hand. That's where the Bhagavad Gita begins, weapons about to be loosed. Gandhi, the man the world knew for nonviolence, kept this book close and called it a guide for his life. How does a man of peace live by a book set on a battlefield?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE GAP BETWEEN THEM.` → `ARJUNA'S BOW SLIPS.` → `A MAN OF PEACE, A BOOK OF WAR?`

segments.voice: Gandhi made his own version of the Gita in Gujarati and called it Anasakti Yoga. In its introduction he says that he didn't read the war as history. He read the field as the human heart. The two armies, in his reading, are the forces of good and evil inside one person, and the battle is the one each of us fights there. Krishna, the charioteer, is for him the dweller within, the voice that speaks from the inside. So when Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up and fight, Gandhi hears: don't run from the struggle inside you. A text that seems to send a man into battle becomes, in his hands, a handbook for a nonviolent life. After years of trying to live the Gita's teaching, he wrote, he found its complete selflessness isn't possible without nonviolence. This is one reading among several. Other readers, traditional commentators among them, take the war as a real war and Arjuna's duty as a warrior's real duty: Krishna tells a soldier to do what his role asks, without hatred and without clinging to victory. Still others hold both at once, a real field and a mirror of the inner one. The Gita's first line names the place twice: dharmakshetra, kurukshetra. The field of dharma, the field of the Kurus. Read Gandhi's way, the first name carries the weight: the field of right living is the ground between what a person wants to do and what they know is right.
screen: `HE READ THE FIELD AS THE HEART.` · `KRISHNA: THE DWELLER WITHIN.` · `ONE READING AMONG SEVERAL.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA, THE FIELD OF THE KURUS.` · then, large: `THE BATTLE IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small battle you're in: something you want to say and suspect you shouldn't, or something you know is right and keep putting off. Do what Arjuna did, and drive out into the gap to look at both sides calmly, the side that pulls on the in-breath, the side that asks on the out-breath, without choosing yet. If you pray, you can hold the whole field before Krishna, or before the one you pray to.
Gandhi's Gita. The Bhagavad Gita as Gandhi read it: a battle fought inside the heart, with Krishna as the voice within.
Your line: the battle is inside. Tomorrow, the one word Gandhi put on the cover. That's day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: The work, not the fruit
958.hook: the word Gandhi put on the cover: anasakti
958.carry: your right is to the work, not its fruit
958.howItsDone: Some who follow the Gita's path of action try to offer their daily work without clinging to its results, and some readers of Gandhi pair Gita 2:47 with his line that means and ends are like seed and tree.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the battlefield moved inside: Gandhi read the Gita's field as the human heart, and Krishna as the dweller within. The battle is inside.

Arjuna stands between the two armies with his bow on the ground. He can see how this might end: teachers dead, cousins dead, a kingdom won and nothing worth having in it. Fear of the outcome has frozen him. In the second chapter, Krishna's answer holds one of the best-known verses in the whole Gita. When Gandhi made his own Gita in Gujarati, he didn't name it after Krishna or after the battle. He named it after the idea in that verse.
screen: `ARJUNA, FROZEN BY THE OUTCOME.` → `ONE VERSE IN THE SECOND CHAPTER.` → `THE WORD ON THE COVER.`

segments.voice: The title is Anasakti Yoga. Anasakti is usually put into English as non-attachment, or selfless action: doing the work without clinging to what it gets you. Gandhi said this was the Gita's central teaching, the one the rest of the book circles around. It's gathered in that verse, where Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting. And don't cling to doing nothing, either. That last part closes the easy exit. Letting go of the fruit is not walking away from the field. Many Hindu families know it by its opening words, karmanye vadhikaraste; it's a verse grandparents still quote before a big exam. Gandhi pushed against a misreading here. Non-attachment, he wrote, doesn't mean not caring how things turn out. The one who lets go of the fruit is wholly given to doing the task well, because nothing is being saved up for the reward. In a little book called Hind Swaraj, he had a picture for this. The means are like a seed, and the end like a tree. You can't plant one kind of seed and expect another kind of tree. So if you care about the end, care first about the means, the part actually in your hands. Now Arjuna's freeze makes sense. He can't control how the war ends. He can do his part, with full care. Anasakti is exactly that: the work given wholly, the fruit let go.
screen: `ANASAKTI: NOT CLINGING TO THE FRUIT.` · `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE WORK ALONE.` · `KARMANYE VADHIKARASTE.` · `LETTING GO IS NOT NOT CARING.` · `THE MEANS ARE A SEED, THE END A TREE.` · then, large: `THE WORK IS YOURS. LET THE FRUIT GO.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you're working on, a project, a conversation you hope goes well, a person you're trying to help, and notice how much of your mind is already standing at the finish line. Walk it gently back to the one small step in your hands today, and on each out-breath set the result down, like a bag you've been carrying. If you pray, you can offer the work, and its fruit, to Krishna, or to the one you pray to.
Gandhi's Gita. He called it Anasakti Yoga: the work given fully, the fruit let go.
Your line: your right is to the work, not its fruit. Tomorrow, how a wise person walks. See you then.

959.title: How a wise person walks
959.hook: how does a person of steady wisdom walk?
959.carry: steady wisdom: draw in like the tortoise
959.howItsDone: Some Hindus learn the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the person of steady wisdom, by heart and recite them as a daily reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word on the cover of Gandhi's Gita: anasakti. Your right is to the work, not its fruit.

How does a wise person walk? It sounds like a riddle, but it's Arjuna's real question near the end of the Gita's second chapter. Krishna has just described a person whose understanding is steady, and Arjuna wants specifics. How do they speak? How do they sit? How do they walk? Krishna's answer is the portrait we met three days ago, the one Gandhi kept coming back to. Today we read it slowly, on our last day with Gandhi's Gita.
screen: `HOW DOES A WISE PERSON WALK?` → `ARJUNA WANTS SPECIFICS.` → `THE PERSON OF STEADY WISDOM.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit name for this person is sthitaprajna, one whose wisdom stands firm. In paraphrase: such a person is content in the Self alone. Sorrow doesn't shake them, pleasure doesn't grab them, and they're free of craving, fear and anger. Then the first image: like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, they can draw the senses back from the things that pull at them. Not destroying the senses. Drawing them in, when needed. Krishna doesn't pretend it's easy. Someone who simply goes without may keep away from what they want, but the taste for it stays behind. Only when the highest is seen does even the taste fall away. Then a stranger picture. What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake in, and what everyone else is awake to is night for the one who sees. The portrait ends with the sea. Rivers pour into the ocean all the time, and it stays full and unmoved. So is the one into whom desires flow without disturbing them. That one finds peace. Gandhi held this passage close. On his reading, the battlefield is the heart. Anasakti is how to work on that field without clinging to the fruit. And the sthitaprajna is what a person looks like after long practice: still walking, still speaking, still in the world, but steady, like the sea.
screen: `STHITAPRAJNA: WISDOM THAT STANDS FIRM.` · `LIKE A TORTOISE DRAWING IN ITS LIMBS.` · `THE TASTE STAYS BEHIND.` · `RIVERS POUR IN; THE SEA STAYS STILL.` · then, large: `STEADY, LIKE THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Notice the senses one at a time, the sounds in the room, the light on your eyelids, the feel of the chair, and draw your attention back from each, the way a tortoise draws in a foot, until what's left is the breath. If something you want pulls you back out, notice that the taste is still there and let it sit without following it, while you picture the sea staying level as the rivers come in. If you pray, you can rest in Krishna, or in the one you pray to, as the still water.
Gandhi's Gita. The heart as the battlefield, anasakti as the way to work, and the person of steady wisdom, unmoved like the sea, as the goal.
